newsitem.title: HUNGARY: FEATURE - Alcoa makes Russian connection in Hungary.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Alcoa makes Russian connection in Hungary.

text.p: Gleaming red Coca Cola trucks, made with Russian aluminium and equipped with special heaters to keep drinks from freezing in Siberia, roll off an Alcoa assembly line in Hungary.
In another age, the aluminium probably would have gone into a Tupolev bomber, but today it is being used by an American company to build beverage trucks for the Russian market.
"There was a lot of Russian metal that was basically being used for the defence industry," said Ralph Matera, general manager of the Alcoa-Kofem Kft plant 80 km (50 miles) west of Budapest.

"When that collapsed, there was all this metal available and basically metal for Russia is hard currency," Matera said, adding that the end of the Cold War also made a neat fit for Alcoa, which wanted to expand in Europe.
"They (the Russians) started exporting to the West...and we wanted to expand through acquisitions. We wanted to get things that fit into our business and not add a lot of capacity."
That piece of the puzzle was provided by Hungary, which in 1993 sold a 50.1 share of its formerly state-owned Kofem aluminium fabricating plant to Alcoa for $50 million.
Alcoa paid another $25 million for the remaining portion of the plant last year, and has invested some $75 million more to refurbish and upgrade it, Matera said.
"It's been a struggle," Matera, who took over as general manager last year, told Reuters.
"We've not made any money in the first three years, although this year we should make some. We bought facilities that were obviously under-performing.

"I think that when you look at this facility probably for the 10 to 15 years prior to us purchasing it there wasn't any cash. The facility was run down, maintenance wasn't done. It was old and equipment wasn't updated.
"So we've had to invest a lot into it. But Alcoa's made a commitment to the area and Alcoa right now in Hungary employs more than 7,000 people and that could grow in the near future."
The company said it reported a loss of 2.67 billion forints ($16.2 million) on revenues of 35.7 billion forints ($216.68 million).
POISED TO BECOME MAJOR EUROPEAN PLAYER
But the improvements can be seen everywhere around the 82 hectare (202-acre) complex and Alcoa-Kofem seems poised to become a major player in the European market.

One of the buildings is being renovated for use by Alcoa's forged wheels division and will soon be producing 250,000 forged aluminium wheels a year for the European bus and truck market. The investment there is another $39.5 million on top of the money ploughed into Alcoa-Kofem.
John Kromberg, general manager of Alcoa Wheel Products Europe Ltd, said the plant would take over many European customers from Alcoa's U.S. wheel division.
"Our major customers are the European market -- Mercedes, Volvo and Renault, but we will also ship these wheels to Brazil, Australia and Japan," Kromberg said.
John Hussa, the manager for end products who is in charge of truck body assemblies, said Alcoa hopes to corner the European market for aluminium-bodied beverage delivery trucks.

"We're just finishing up a major order (for Coca Cola) and then we're starting a prototype that we've developed ourselves with a different type of door opening," Hussa said during a tour of the plant.
"We expect to ship between 600 and 800 of these units this year...but we're expecting pretty much a chain reaction because when one company sees the units it spreads pretty quickly," he said.
OTHER PRODUCTS

In addition, Alcoa-Kofem produces what Matera calls the "standard vanilla" products of the industry: corrugated sheets, window and door frames, lamp poles, finned tubing for heaters and air conditioners and a wide range of other products.
Most of the raw material is Russian metal because it is cheaper, quality is good and, perhaps most important, it's available in large quantities, Matera said.

"Demand for metal in Europe is about four million tonnes per year and the capacity is three million tonnes," he said. "So there is a net inflow of metal into Europe and a big part of that is coming from Russia.
"We're in a situation right now where we can bring metal in, add value to it and re-export to the West," he said, adding that Alcoa-Kofem imports about 100,000 tonnes of aluminium a year.

Alcoa is, however, negotiating with the government over a change in regulations due to take effect on July 1 that would eliminate drawbacks on customs fees and duties. Matera said the change could cost Alcoa $10 million a year.

"Any changes in duties, anything that affects the cost of our metal purchases -- being that they're such a high percentage of our cost to goods sold -- has a very serious effect on our business," Matera said.
"Hopefully these changes as Hungary moves into the EU will not hurt companies like ourselves that are doing business here and have made a big commitment."
